title: Summative Portfolio
text:
Word Count and Deadline

Word count: 2,400 words (±10%). Three equally weighted components, with a recommended word count of 800 words each.
Deadline: 12 noon, 9th December 2026

The portfolio provides an opportunity to explore an analysis focus of your choice, using analyses of selected digital data to answer analysis questions. ‘Analysis focus’ here refers to a broad research problem, area for exploration, intellectual puzzle, or similar.
Component 1 sets out the overall analysis focus, data selection and management, analysis approaches used, and reflections appropriate to these.
Components 2 and 3 present two distinct write-ups of findings and reflections, and, taken together, should incorporate both qualitative and quantitative analysis.
Across the course, you will have opportunity to undertake different forms of analysis with different qualitative and quantitative datasets. You can select which elements from these to develop and write-up. It is also permitted to use analysis approaches and data beyond what is directly covered on the course. If considering the latter, please confirm choices with staff during the labs, via email, or at Office Hours.

Component 1: Analysis Design
Provide a succinct analysis design that covers the key data and analysis decisions which informed the findings presented in components 2 and 3.
Your analysis design must include the following:
Analysis Focus (~150 words): Briefly introduce your analysis focus through 3-5 references to relevant theoretical and empirical sources.
Data Selection and Preparation (~150 words): Explain and justify your selection of digital data; how you collected it; and, how you organised and prepared it for analysis.
Analysis Approaches (~300 words): Set out the analysis approaches used and explain their suitability for your analysis focus and selected digital data.
Reflections (~200 words): Discuss relevant ethical and reflexive considerations for your data and analysis decisions.
Important for the analysis design is demonstrating alignment across these sections. For example, it should be clear to a reader how the analysis focus informed data and analysis decisions made.


Component 2 & 3: Analysis Findings
Present two distinct write-ups of analysis findings.
Begin each component with approximately 200 words to set out the analysis question it seeks to answer and considerations of the data analysed. The latter should draw on relevant concepts, theory, and/or methods texts to consider how the digital data was produced, what it records or represents, and how this shaped your analysis and interpretation of findings.
Then use approximately 600 words to present and interpret selected findings that contribute towards answering the analysis question. Alongside these findings, reflect on your exploration of the data. For example, any unexpected findings, limitations encountered, or what the analysis suggests about the value of the data and analysis approach for investigating your analysis focus.

Choosing and presenting your analyses
The findings should demonstrate range in analysis approach and not reuse the same approaches. Combined, they must also include findings from quantitative and qualitative approaches. However, there remains flexibility in how to achieve this, with valid combinations including:

one component quantitative and the other qualitative
one component quantitative or qualitative and the other mixed methods
both components providing mix of quantitative and qualitative analysis findings

However, please note: If you have been asked by the Scottish Graduate School to focus particularly on quantitative or qualitative approaches, both components can be quantitative or qualitative.
Your analysis findings may use the same digital data for both or work with different sources of data.
You should cite relevant theoretical or empirical literature to contextualise your findings.
Given word counts, analysis findings should contribute towards answering the analysis questions, but it is not expected that they will answer them in full.
To support and evidence your analysis findings, write-ups must include any figures and text excerpts relevant for presenting findings for your chosen analysis approaches. Figures and excerpts will not be included in word counts, but all figures and excerpts presented must be sufficiently discussed within the main text.
Code is not assessed as part of the portfolio and should not be included as part of the portfolio.

text:
Creating an R Markdown file
There are two main ways to create an R Markdown file in RStudio, and they give you slightly different files.
After creating a new markdown file, RStudio may display a yellow banner at the top of the file asking to install some packages (the rmarkdown package and the additional packages it needs): click ‘Yes’. (Don’t worry if this doesn’t show: if the packages are already installed, there is nothing for RStudio to ask).
From the File menu
From the menu bar at the top of RStudio, select File > New File > R Markdown....


File > New File > R Markdown…


From the top menu-bar select ‘File’.
In the File menu, select the first item ‘New File’.
In the New File sub-menu, select ‘R Markdown…’.

A ‘New R Markdown’ dialogue window will open. Type a title in the ‘Title’ section and your name in the ‘Author’ box. (Optionally) tick the checkbox for ‘Use current date when rendering document’. The ‘Default Output Format’ as HTML is fine for what we cover on the module. Then, click ‘OK’.


The New R Markdown dialogue.

Important. After creating the new file is not actually saved yet. Save it with File > Save As..., and give it a name. RStudio will auto-add .Rmd to the end.
When creating a new R Markdown file via the File menu, it includes some template content by default: a YAML header with the title, name of the author, date, and the type of output; a code chunk named “setup”; and, some example text and code chunks going over the basics of R Markdown.


A new R Markdown file created from the File menu, with its example content.

The example content is useful to look at once (the setup chunk is explained on the Code chunks page), but you will usually delete everything below the setup chunk before starting your own work.
From the Files pane
Within the Files pane (in the bottom-right section in RStudio):

Click ‘New File’.
From the list of options select ‘R Markdown’.



New File > R Markdown in the Files pane.

Within the ‘Create a New File in Current Directory’ dialogue that pops up:

Give the file an appropriate name, such as exploratory-analysis.Rmd.
Click ‘OK’.



Naming the new file in the ‘Create a New File in Current Directory’ dialogue.

The R Markdown file will automatically open in the Source pane (top-left). It just contains basic YAML for title and output, which is HTML by default, and by default the title is just the name given to the file. Feel free to then flesh out the YAML header, such as adding a more full descriptive title and your name as the author (see The YAML header).


A new R Markdown file created from the Files pane.







Important



The new file created will be added to whichever folder is currently active within the Files pane. So, before you click ‘New File’, check you are in the folder you want to add the file to. For example, the main top-level folder for your project not a subfolder.

title: R Markdown
text:
Writing text: Markdown syntax
R Markdown uses simple, human-readable syntax for basic formatting. Whilst different to how you would write text in a Word document, it is easy to learn. (The R Markdown cheat sheet, available from RStudio via Help > Cheat Sheets also gives a single-page summary of the syntax.)
Headings
Headings are created by using the pound / hash sign, #, at the start of a line, with the number of hashes determining the header level:
# Heading 1

## Heading 2

### Heading 3

#### Heading 4

##### Heading 5

###### Heading 6
And, how it appears when knitted:


The six heading levels when knitted.

Bold, italics, and lists
Basic formatting and lists similarly use simple ‘markup’ such as * and -:
Single asterisks creates *italicised* and double asterisks
creates **bold** text.

- Dashes `-` create lists.
  - Add spaces at start of line before the dash.
  - To create indented lists.

1. Adding numbers at the start.
2. Will create a numbered list.
And, this is how it appears when knitted:


The formatting example when knitted.

Blank lines between paragraphs, lists and headers
The main thing in R Markdown’s syntax that trips up new users is the requirement to have empty line spaces between:

Each paragraph
Before and after a list
Before and after a header
Before and after a code chunk

Here’s some example text in an R Markdown document, the first without line spacing, the second with:
When knitted the below text
# will not appear as a header
because there is no line spacing

When knitted the below text

# will appear as a header

because there is line spacing
And, how this looks when knitted:


The same above text when knitted.







NoteAside: where the empty lines come from





This practice of using empty line spaces originates from traditional coding conventions. To make code readable, a common coding convention is to place a specified limit on the number of characters per line, with any text beyond that number placed on a new line. Whilst that works OK for code, it creates an issue for text as we now need to distinguish a new line used simply to keep the number of characters per line to a set number and a new line meant to designate a new paragraph, start of a list, and similar. The solution decided upon is to have an empty line.
Additional aside: If you have encountered Markdown in other software, you may have come across exceptions to this convention. Some contemporary apps that are focused more on writing than coding do away with the need for empty lines before lists and other elements, adding to the confusion when using R Markdown for the first time when empty lines are required.



Why # is a header outside a code chunk but a comment inside one
# Data Cleaning

## Coercing the age variable

```{r coerce-age}
# age is read in as text, so need to transform the variable to numeric
police <- police |> mutate(age = as.numeric(age))
```
In the above we can see how:

Outside a code chunk, # creates a level 1 header and ## creates a level 2 header.
Inside the code chunk, the # creates a comment.

Any text within an R code chunk after a # is treated as a comment and is not run as part of the code (see Comments on the R syntax page).
You may be wondering why the same character gets used in two different ways. The reason is that R and Markdown developed separately to each other. By the time R Markdown was created to bring the two together, they both had already decided to use # for different things. Inside of a code chunk, all text is treated as code for the language specified in the curly brackets, e.g. ```{r}. In R, hash signs are used for comments, so they are treated as comments when inside the code chunk rather than as Markdown headers. Whilst confusing at first, it all boils down to “# inside code chunk = comments” and “# outside code chunks = headers”.
So if you want a new section in your document, the heading goes in the regular text, not in a code chunk: a line such as ## Categorical analysis typed inside a chunk is just a comment, and no heading will display in the knitted file.

title: R Markdown
text:
The YAML header
The part at the top of an R Markdown file enclosed by the dashes --- is called YAML. YAML is a simple human-readable markup language for data serialisation, often used with Markdown as it provides a simple human-readable structure for adding metadata, such as the document title, author, date, and desired output when knitting. It consists of what are referred to as key: value pairs.
The YAML block must be at the very top of the document, so do not add any new lines before it. Two common issues for beginners is either (1) accidentally adding new lines before the YAML header or (2) accidentally deleting the opening or closing --- that enclose the YAML header.


Template

---
title: "TITLE"
author: "YOUR_NAME"
date: "20/11/26"
output: html_document
---



title is self-explanatory, simply replace TITLE with the title of the document you are working on.

author again simply replace YOUR_NAME with your name.

date can be any text. However, format(Sys.time(), '%d/%m/%y')is a nice single line of R code that runs when the file is knitted to retrieve the current date and formats it as dd/mm/yy, such as 04/12/26. This then effectively makes the date field “date this file was knitted” and saves you having to manually update it each time (see An automatic date).

output specifies what file format(s) to output to when knitting the R Markdown file.

Whilst quotation marks - " - are not always needed for text fields like title, author, and date, but it is always best practice to include i anyway. For example, title: some title would work without quotation marks, but title: some title: and its subtitle would not due to confusion over the additional :. With quotation marks though, title: "some title: and its subtitle" would work as the " makes clear the second : is part of the title text. Note though that html_document is not ‘text’ - as in text to display - but an ‘option’ so it never has quotation marks around it.
In RStudio it looks like this:


A YAML header in RStudio.

An automatic date
The date line in the YAML header above used inline code by exclosing code inside `r and a closing `.
This meant we could include the following code to automatically get today’s date each time we knit the document:

format(Sys.time(), '%d/%m/%y')


The format() function takes an object as its first argument and then one or more further arguments to specify how it should be formatted.
The Sys.time() function checks the date and time on the device and creates a ‘date time object’ (basically an R object which stores a date and time) with the current date and time.
Our last bit of code then, '%d/%m/%y', specifies the format the date time object should be displayed in. The % followed by a letter specifies which date/time info to include, and how to format it, from our date time object: %d the day, %m the month and %y the year as two digits. For the year in four digits, such as 2026, use %Y instead.







NoteAside, why we need format()





If you run Sys.time() in the Console, you will see the date is formatted Year-Month-Day:

Sys.time()

[1] "2026-11-20 15:48:39 GMT"


This is common in computing as if you have a list of dates and sort them this will work, whereas if it was Day-Month-Year it would put 1st October before 5th May because 1 comes before 5.
format() then let’s us transform how the date is displayed to order people are more used to:

format(Sys.time(), '%d/%m/%y')

[1] "20/11/26"


You can run help(format.POSIXct) in the Console and scroll down a bit in the help page to see what other % options are available. (POSIXct is just the class type of the date time object we created, with ‘ct’ standing for calendar time.)



Options for HTML documents
We can do a lot with the YAML header. A nested list of additional key-value pairs under html_document: can be used to specify some options for how we want a knitted HTML document to look:
---
title: "R Markdown Test"
subtitle: "This is a test"
author: "Your Name Here"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: true
    theme: cosmo
date: "2026-11-20"
---


html_document goes on its own line under output:, with a 2-space indent at the start and a : at the end. (In RStudio, placing your cursor at the start of html_document and hitting enter should auto-add the 2-space indent for you.)
The options for the HTML document go on the lines under it, each now with a 4-space indent to make clear these are key-value pairs related to html_document:.

toc stands for “table of contents” and is false by default.

toc_float places the table of contents as a floating element on the left-hand side of the document rather than as fixed text at the top of the document.

theme changes the default HTML template used to the “cosmo” theme instead.

date: as it is a main option - and not a sub-option of output: nor html_document: - appears at start of a new line with no indent.



YAML header with additional key value pairs.

The knitted document would contain the main title, subtitle, followed by your name and the current date, as specified in the YAML. A table of contents appears on the left, showing the headers used in the document, with the header for the section currently in view on the screen highlighted in blue (notice how it changes if you scroll up/down the HTML file).


A knitted R Markdown document with a floating table of contents.

This is another powerful aspect of using R Markdown. Your document itself remains fairly simple, but with a few simple options you can quickly customise its look and add features like a table of contents. There are a lot more options you can use with HTML documents and a range of themes you can choose from.

title: R Markdown
text:
Knitting
Knitting a document runs all your R code from top to bottom, then combines the results from this with the Markdown text to convert these into different file formats. YAML is used to specify which file formats to convert to. To render the document from R Markdown to HTML, click on the ‘Knit’ button at the top of the file (or press Ctrl-Shift-KCtrl-Shift-K).


The Knit button.

The first time you knit, and if you have not done so already, RStudio may ask you if you want to install or update some packages: click ‘Yes’. After you knit the document, a window with the output will pop up automatically. You can come back to the R Markdown file to make changes and knit it again as many times as you wish. Importantly though, knitting is not automatic: each time you change the R Markdown file you will need to ‘knit’ it again for the changes to be reflected in the HTML file.
The knitted HTML file
When you knit a document as a HTML file, RStudio actually creates a new .html file with the same name as your R Markdown document, in the same folder. You can confirm this by looking in the ‘Files’ tab in the bottom-right.


The knitted RMarkdown.html beside RMarkdown.Rmd in the Files pane.

To open the knitted file again later, click its name in the Files pane and choose ‘View in Web Browser’.
The Knit menu: HTML, PDF and Word
The small arrow beside the Knit button opens a menu with ‘Knit to HTML’, ‘Knit to PDF’ and ‘Knit to Word’.


The Knit button’s menu.

Choosing one of these also adds it to the output: line of your YAML header. Say you select PDF, pdf_document will be added to output: in the YAML header. Now every time that you knit, an HTML file and a PDF file will be created. That’s fine if that is what you intended, but can come as a surprise if not.
Importantly, this behaviour can result in unexpected issues if you are using a package whose output does not work nicely with your chosen format. Some R table packages, for example, require additional setup if wanting to knit to PDF. It is surprisingly easy to accidentally click ‘Knit to PDF’ and have pdf_document added to the YAML header, resulting in a file that used to knit without issue not failing to knit. To fix such issues, all you need to do is remove the pdf_document line from the YAML header.
Knitting starts from a clean R session
Importantly, when you knit an R Markdown document, all code is run sequentially from top to bottom in a fresh R session - in other words, it starts with a blank Global Environment. This ensures the document is reproducible. Anyone with a copy of the R Markdown file and the data being used should be able to knit it and receive the exact same results.
This requires though that all essential code for your analysis is within code chunks and in the correct order that they need to be run in. For example, if you run d <- 25 manually in the Console and then add d + 5 in a code chunk, that code chunk will work fine when manually run in RStudio, but will result in an “object not found” error if you try to knit. This is because d <- 25 also needs to be in a code chunk before the d + 5 code within the R Markdown file as the clean Global Environment used to knit will not have an object called d.
The same applies to packages and data. Whilst knitting can access packages that are installed on the computer, it has no packages loaded nor data frames read in. Even data frames sitting in your Global Environment (the top-right pane) from earlier work are not available to clean Global Environment used when knitting a file. This is why it is important to include a code chunk at the top of your document that loads all required packages and reads in your data.

title: R Markdown
text:
Knitting Errors
An object or function not found
If you receive an object '...' not found error when knitting, for an object you can see in your Environment pane, it is likely the code that creates it was run in the Console, or in a chunk you have since changed or deleted, rather than in the file (see Knitting starts from a clean R session above). Likewise, if you receive could not find function "...", it is likely the package the function comes is not loaded in a code chunk within the file:
Error in `read_csv()`:
! could not find function "read_csv"

Quitting from analysis.Rmd:6-8 [preamble]
Execution halted
The “Quitting from” line gives the file, the lines of the code chunk (here lines 6-8) and, in square brackets, the chunk’s label (preamble). A chunk without a label is listed as unnamed-chunk-1, unnamed-chunk-2 and so on, which is one reason labels are worth adding (see Chunk labels).
The solution for the above would be to add the missing code that would load the package which provides the read_csv() function - e.g. library(tidyverse) - in a code chunk before read_csv() is first used.
PDF in the output
A common cause of knitting issues is accidentally adding PDF as a file format to output when knitting. If receiving a “package ‘…’ could not be loaded” error message, check the YAML header at the top of your R Markdown file. Some R table packages require additional code when knitting to PDF, without which your file will fail to knit with vague error messages.
You should have either of the following for output: ...:


Either

output: html_document



Or

output:
  html_document:
    ...

But, will probably have something like the following if receiving the error message:
output:
  pdf_document: default
  html_document: default
This can happen unintentionally as RStudio can automatically add a line for PDF output, such as if you accidentally clicked ‘Knit to PDF’ in the Knit menu. Annoyingly, even if you click ‘Knit to HTML’ from the options, if your YAML header includes pdf_document in its outputs, R will still try to create a PDF document and keep running into the error message.
So, if you are receiving the error message and have the two output lines, you can easily fix it by removing the pdf_document line. As the YAML header then specifies an HTML output, you can just click the ‘Knit’ button directly each time rather than clicking the wee down arrow to select ‘Knit to HTML’ specifically.
The file is in the wrong folder
If code that reads your data works in one R Markdown file but gives an error in another, the most likely cause is that the second file was created in a subfolder, rather than the top-level project folder.


The Files pane showing the data subfolder, with project highlighted in the folder path.

The reason is that an R Markdown file runs its code from its own folder. Code like read_csv("data/police_killings.csv") looks for a data folder inside the folder the .Rmd is in. So if our R Markdown file was accidentally saved in the data subfolder, R looks for our csv file at data/data/police_killings.csv, which does not exist:
Error:
! 'data/police_killings.csv' does not exist in current working
  directory:
  '.../project/data'.
The fix is to move the R Markdown file up to the top-level project folder (see Moving files on the RStudio page). File paths and the working directory are explained on the Base R page.
Two chunks with the same label
Chunk labels are optional, but each label can only be used once in a file. It is easy to end up with two when copying and tweaking an existing chunk, such as a second setup chunk copied with its label, and this stops the knit before any code runs:
Error in parse_block(g[-1], g[1], params.src, markdown_mode) :
  Duplicate chunk label 'setup', which has been used for the chunk:
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
Calls: <Anonymous> ... process_file -> split_file -> lapply -> FUN -> parse_block
Execution halted
Despite the confusing error message, the solution is simple: rename or delete the label for one of the code chunks and the file will knit again.

title: Code chunks
text: A code chunk is a “fenced” block (it is enclosed above and below with ```) in an R Markdown file for adding R code. These can then be run within RStudio and are used when ‘knitting’ R Markdown files to HTML, PDF, or Word documents.

title: Code chunks
text:
Writing a code chunk

The parts of a code chunk
In most colour schemes, code chunks have a different shaded background in RStudio. If using the default light colour scheme the background is a light gray.
The general shape of a code chunk:


Template

```{r CHUNK_NAME, OPTION = VALUE}
# (optionally) use '#' at start of line to add comments
CODE
```


Three back-ticks open the chunk with curly brackets to specify {programming-language optional-name, any-options = values}.
Since we are using R, all our code chunks have {r ...}. CHUNK_NAME (the ‘label’) and OPTION = VALUE are both optional. A chunk takes one label at most, but can take several options, separated by commas (see Chunk labels and Chunk options).
Within code chunks, the pound sign / hash, #, at the start of a line is used to add any comments (see Comments on the R syntax page, and, for why # makes a header outside a chunk instead, the R Markdown page]).
CODE is your R code, as many lines of it as the chunk needs - which varies but a general rough rule of thumb would be to put each logical unit of code together in a code chunk.
Three back-ticks on a line of their own close the chunk.

The ` is called a back-tick, and on contemporary UK keyboards is under the Esc key / to the left of the number 1 key.



A code chunk named optional-name under a header.




Inserting a chunk
To create a new code chunk, you have four options:

Put your text cursor on a line in your R Markdown file and press Ctrl-Alt-ICtrl-Alt-I on the keyboard.
From the menu bar at the top of RStudio, you can select Code > Insert Chunk.
Click on the icon that is a c in a green square with a ‘+’ in a circle in its top-left corner, and then click on R to create an R code chunk. (Sorry - see screenshot below - as you’ll notice when find it on the screen, it’s bit hard to describe it clearly!)
Manually type three back-ticks and then {r} (remember to add three back-ticks on a line below to close the code chunk as well).




Using the ‘c’ icon to create a new code chunk.




Chunk labels
Chunk labels are added straight after the r in the code chunk, e.g. {r optional-name}, and have multiple purposes:

A quick way to remind yourself the purpose of each code chunk.
The menu in the bar along the bottom of the Source pane also shows the name of the chunk or section your cursor is in, such as “Chunk 1: sum-1”, and can be used to jump to specific sections and code chunks in your document. So, if you provide a label for your code chunk it will also appear there.
When a file fails to knit, the error message also gives the label of the chunk where the error occurred.

Two things though to be aware of with labels:

Each label can be used only once in a file; a second chunk with the same label stops the file from knitting (see Two chunks with the same label).
Write labels with hyphens rather than spaces, as in optional-name. A label with a space will usually still knit, but labels are used in the file names of the plots a chunk makes, and R Markdown: The Definitive Guide recommends only letters, numbers and dashes, as spaces and underscores may cause trouble in some packages.

Unlike the name of an object, a label is not used anywhere else in your code, so a typo in one does no harm, as long as it doesn’t make two labels the same.

title: Code chunks
text:
Running code chunks
There are multiple ways to run your R code.

Running a chunk
To run a code chunk, you can click on the Run green arrow situated on the top right corner of it. Alternatively, if your text cursor is inside the code chunk you can press Ctrl-Alt-CCtrl-Alt-C on your keyboard.



Run current code chunk button.


For the chunk sum-1 in the screenshot, which runs 2 + 2, what you will see after running the chunk is:

In the R Markdown file, [1] 4 underneath the code chunk.
In the Console, both > 2 + 2 and [1] 4.




Output in R Markdown file and Console after running a code chunk.


Why do we see this? When you run a chunk, RStudio sends the code to the Console for R to run it, so you see the code echoed and its raw output there. RStudio also shows the results inline under the chunk so you can see the output in context. (This also becomes important with graphs and formatted tables that cannot be viewed in the Console.) (What the [1] means is explained on the R syntax page.)


Running all chunks above
Within the top-right of each code chunk there are two buttons:

Run All Chunks Above - the downward facing grey arrow/triangle with a green line under it, which will run all code chunks from the top of your document down to this code chunk.
Run Current Chunk - the green arrow/triangle, which will run the code within that code chunk only.




‘Run All Chunks Above’ (1) and ‘Run Current Chunk’ (2).


The first is useful when a code chunk depends upon others being run first, and when a code chunk that was previously working suddenly returns unexpected results or an error message (see running your code again from the top for why). Thankfully, RStudio makes this easy to do: click (1) ‘Run All Chunks Above’, then (2) ‘Run Current Chunk’. It is also useful if you restart your R environment, losing the results of previously run code, and need to re-run everything before this chunk.


The Run menu
Further options can be found in the ‘Run’ drop-down menu, accessed from the top-right of the Source pane by clicking the small downwards pointing black triangle on the ‘Run’ button:



The Run button’s drop-down menu.


Useful additional ones here are:

Run Selected Line(s) - running all lines you have manually selected using the mouse / text cursor, or the line your text cursor is on (Ctrl-EnterCtrl-Enter).
Restart R and Run All Chunks - incredibly useful when you need to reset your R environment. It also runs the file the way knitting does, from a clean R session, so it helps in finding and fixing issues that would stop the file from knitting.

Note as well that many of these options have keyboard shortcuts listed (the menu shows the Windows ones; on a Mac they use Command and Option instead).

title: Code chunks
text:
Chunk options
Options are used to specify how code chunks are handled when run/knitted.

Setting options


Template

```{r CHUNK_NAME, OPTION1 = VALUE1, OPTION2 = VALUE2, ...}
CODE
```

Options go inside the curly brackets, after the language and any label. A chunk can take one option or several, separated by commas (... simply means “and so on”; don’t type it). Their values are usually TRUE or FALSE, such as echo = FALSE.
Some key options that you can set for code chunks - either globally in the setup code chunk or on a per code chunk basis - are:

echo

whether the code chunk is shown in knitted files.

include

whether the code chunk and its output - such as tables and graphs - are displayed in knitted files. include=FALSE means the code should be run, but the code chunk and any output should not be included in the knitted file.

message and warning

whether messages and warnings raised when running code are displayed in knitted files.

eval

whether the code is run or not.


By default, the code chunk and the output are displayed in knitted files. Examples when working in an R Markdown document:



Three chunks running the same sumtable() code with no options, echo=FALSE and include=FALSE.


And when knitted:



The three chunks when knitted.


Setting eval=FALSE is useful if wanting to include example code or code that would result in an error message. This makes it incredibly useful when writing your own notes as - for example - you can keep a record of code that resulted in an error message followed by another code chunk that has the working code.
Importantly, showing the code from your code chunks in your knitted files is what makes the files and their knitted outputs useful reference material, such as notes on what you have learnt. When writing academic articles and research reports for a public audience, though, we usually do not want to include our code, so we use echo=FALSE so we have the tables and graphs without the code that made them.






NoteAside: #| options





You may also come across options written on lines at the top of the chunk, each starting with #|. This does the same as writing them inside the curly brackets, and works in R Markdown files with more recent versions of the knitr package.
Note the different way of writing the values: false rather than FALSE, and a colon rather than =:
```{r counts}
#| echo: false
count(police, raceethnicity)
```

The above is the same as writing {r counts, echo=FALSE}.
However, a line starting #| holds only one option.
All #| lines must come first in the chunk, before any code.

The reason for this is #| is the styled used by Quarto. Quarto is similar to R Markdown but with better support for languages beyond R. I am unsure why they also decided to change the option style, but it has been added to new versions of knitr for R Markdown too for consistency. However, most online R Markdown resources still show the {r OPTIONS} version rather than #|.





Setup code chunk
Rather than adding the same options to every chunk, a code chunk named “setup” at the top of the file, just after the YAML header, can set global default options for all our code chunks. By global, what we mean is that the options set here will apply to all of our code chunks - unless we set individual options for any of them. For example, if you set option=FALSE globally, but needed it to be TRUE for one specific code chunk, all you need to do is add option=TRUE to that specific code chunk’s options to override the global default.
This may look intimidating, but it is relatively simple when parsed bit by bit:
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

The setup after r names the chunk ‘setup’. The include=FALSE after a comma then tells R we do not want the code nor its output for this setup code chunk to show in our knitted files.
knitr is the package used to knit R Markdown files.
knitr::opts_chunk is an object that stores default settings applied to all code chunks. (If you do not load a package directly, you can use package::function or package::object to access functions and objects it provides).
knitr::opts_chunk$set(...) runs the set() function to change the knitr::opts_chunk default settings.

So, putting it all together, what the code in the setup chunk does is use the set() function for the code chunk options object (opts_chunk) provided by the knitr package (the package used for ‘knitting’) to set our global option for messages and warnings to FALSE. This means no messages or warnings that code outputs when run will be included in our knitted file. Note, this doesn’t impact things like tables and plots, which will still be included.



The setup chunk in RStudio.


We do this as a lot of code - like when loading the tidyverse - outputs messages and warnings that are (1) safe to ignore and (2) we do not want to see in our knitted files. Without the setup chunk, the text on loading the tidyverse would also appear in the knitted HTML file:



Text shown in a knitted file if messages were not set to FALSE.


If you want no code in your knitted file, you could add echo=FALSE to the options for each individual code chunk. Or… you can simply add it as a global option in the setup code chunk!



echo=FALSE added as a global option in the setup chunk.


If the code from code chunks is then still appearing in your knitted file, check you have not accidentally removed/modified the setup code chunk. If code from a specific code chunk is showing, but not others, then check you have not accidentally added echo=TRUE to its individual options.

title: Code chunks
text:
Preamble Code Chunk
It is good practice to load any required packages and read in any data being used at the top of the R Markdown file, in a code chunk just after the setup chunk (I tend to label this code chunk ‘preamble’). This keeps all package management and data reading in a single location at the start of the document, making it clear to anyone looking at the file which packages are being used. It further ensures that when running/knitting your code all required packages are loaded and data frames created before the rest of your code is run.
So, that gives the general template:


Template

```{r preamble, include=FALSE}
# Load packages
library(PACKAGE_NAME)

# Read data
OBJECT_NAME <- read_csv("data/FILE_NAME.csv")
```


A chunk named preamble, with include=FALSE so the chunk is not included in knitted files (see Chunk options).
One library(PACKAGE_NAME) line for each package the file uses, under a # Load packages comment.
Reading the data and assigning it to a named object, under a # Read data comment. Replace OBJECT_NAME with the name you choose for the data frame, and "FILE_NAME.csv" the file’s name - as well as change data/ if the file is not in a sub-folder named “data”.

For example, if downloaded the police killings data to analyse, the preamble code chunk may look at follows:


Template

```{r preamble, include=FALSE}
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)

# Read data
police <- read_csv("data/police_killings.csv")
```

And a preamble for the NILT 2012 survey, where we want to load the tidyverse, read in the NILT file, and set up a subset with the key variables of interest for our analysis:
```{r preamble, include=FALSE}
# Load Packages
library(tidyverse)

# Read NILT
nilt <- readRDS("data/nilt_r_object.rds")

# Create subset
nilt_subset <- nilt |>
  select(rsex, rage, highqual, religcat, uninatid, ruhappy, rhourswk, persinc2)
```
Every R Markdown file needs its own preamble chunk, even when the packages and data are already in your Environment pane from earlier work. When we knit files it creates a clean R environment: whilst it can access packages that are installed on the computer, it has no packages loaded nor data frames read in (see Knitting starts from a clean R session). This also ensures your R Markdown file will still run without issue if you restart your R session.
We do not need install.packages() in the preamble: we run install.packages("PACKAGE_NAME") in the Console as we only need to install a package once, but load packages with library(PACKAGE_NAME) in a code chunk at the top of the R Markdown file as packages need to be loaded for every R session (see Installing a package and Loading a package on the Base R page). An install.packages() line left in a chunk would install the package all over again every time the chunk runs or the file is knitted. Moving all code for loading packages into this preamble code chunk also means you do not need, and can safely remove, any other library() lines from the rest of your code chunks. This will reduce the risk of encountering error messages and make it easier to debug them if any do occur.

title: RStudio Helper GPT
text:
Below you will find instructions you can copy/paste into the genAI of your choice and which aims to mitigate a lot of the common issues in genAI responses to prompts about R. As this is the first year this module is running, the instructions are a modified version of those used for a ‘custom GPT’ I created on another module. I’ll test it as we go and make tweaks to the instructions if I spot any egregious issues.
To be clear, any genAI use on this course is not limited to the ‘RStudio Helper’ instructions. Instead, it is made available to help you get more useful responses that are also focused on aiding rather than replacing learning. Overtime as you build your data analysis skills and awareness of common issues in genAI responses, you will want to experiment with writing prompts tailored to your own exact needs and use-cases.

title: RStudio Helper GPT
section: What problems does this GPT address?
text:
What problems does this GPT address?
Among the myriad issues with genAI, one particularly annoying one is that they are trained as a ‘delegate-by-default’ to do as much work on behalf of the user as possible.
If you look for it, you’ll notice most genAI responses follow a similar pattern: “short opener acknowledging info from the prompt, work done on behalf of user, suggestions for what else it can do”. An easy way to see this is to prompt genAI “I need help improving the clarity of this paragraph -” along with a paragraph of text. More often than not, it will respond with “Here’s a clearer and more concise version of your paragraph:”, its rewritten version, and end with overly terse explanation for the changes with suggestions of what other changes it could make. Sometimes the response won’t even include an explanation behind the changes.
This issue tends to be worse with coding, where any explanations given tend towards being overly terse and abstract, assuming a reasonable degree of prior knowledge. This can result in misleading and confusing responses as key information useful for beginners gets left out. If anything, this has gotten worse as models have ‘improved’ over time with responses from ‘agentic’ coding agents and ‘thinking’ models reading like cryptic crossword clues.
GenAI similarly has an atrocious habit of directly giving answers and generally lacking any capability to provide information in a way that does not undermine learning. That is before getting to the problems with genAI bullshit, and how responses can be filled with outright misinformation, needlessly complex and over-convoluted code, and fabricating data for analysis over using the data provided.

title: RStudio Helper GPT
text:
Instructions
In the grey box below is a copy of the instructions. In the top-right corner you’ll see a clipboard icon that you can click on to copy the instructions in full to your clipboard.


## Role and General Interaction

RStudio Helper assists social science users in learning R for data analyis. Users are postgraduate Msc and PhD level social science students. Most are new to R and coding in general. They are using RStudio and R Markdown. Users are based in the UK, so use UK measurements.

You provide actionable advice through textbook style explanations and code chunks with detailed accessible documentation that breaks down and explains the code in small logical chunks at a time.

When users provide their own code with an error message or ask about writing code for a specific dataset, you always continue using textbook style examples and accessible documentation to guide users in learning how to debug error messages and write code themselves.

Where appropriate include information relevant for data analysis and interpretation within the social sciences rather than making abstract simplistic statements about 'good' sample sizes and model fit results.

You have an ardent indefatigable desire to aid students learn data analysis, doing so by giving detailed beginner-friendly explanations in a formal but friendly tone that ALWAYS follow the 'Golden Rules' below.

## Golden Rules

Rule one: Support students in their learning, NEVER do the work for them. Under no circumstances do you ever directly fix code provided to you, write exact code for specific datasets that can be copy and pasted, nor interpret statistical results on behalf of the user.

Rule two: Across all forms of response, NEVER use the exact variables and values if these are provided by the user. You can use analogous examples, but keep it general. If a user is asking about a categorical variable on 'religcat' that stores value of respondents' religion, give a textbook example with another categorical variable such as employment. If they mention a variable for number of children, use an example for number of jobs. Never use an overly similar example, such as using 'annual income' in your example if the user mentioned 'income' or 'monthly income'.

Rule three: NEVER interpret specific statistical results for the user. If they provide a copy of a plot, table, or similar, NEVER interpret these for them. Instead give a general textbook explanation for how the type of graph, table, and so on can be interpreted, avoiding the specifics of what was provided to you. Within your explanation follow rule two and NEVER use the same variables and statistical results as provided by the user. For example, if their prompt mentioned employment status, use a different categorical variable for your explanation. Similarly, use different values and statistical results to the ones provided by the user.

Rule four: NEVER assume information about variables mentioned by the user. If a user mentions a variable for 'age' do not write a full response assuming it is interval or categorical. Instead first ask the user to clarify, with details for how they can check using R. Only once you have this information should you provide a full response.

## Contextual Responses

Adapt responses to the context of the learning environment. Write accessible explanations for social science students who are new to using R for data analysis, including base R, R Studio, the tidyverse, and R Markdown. The structure of R Markdown files and code chunks should follow best data analysis and coding practices.

- Either base R or the tidyverse is OK, but be clear which is used in your responses.
- Use vtable or modelsummary for table packages.
- Prefer `|>` over `%>%` for pipes.
- Load the tidyverse rather than any specific individual package from it. For example, if needing ggplot2, load the tidyverse package and explain ggplot2 is part of the tidyverse.
- When loading libraries, ALWAYS explain how to do this through a code chunk at the top of the R Markdown file with a reminder that libraries only need to be loaded once. NEVER provide code for loading libraries and analysis together in one code chunk.
- When appropriate, remind users they can set global options through a code chunk at the top of their R Markdown file.
- Make responses accessible by explaining all R & data analysis terms each time they are first used. Users are new to R & may not know what terms like data frame, library, vector, function, object, plot, & so on mean.
- Refer to relevant panels within RStudio, such as the Environment panel for checking a data frame or when installing a library explain how to install it through RStudio's console. Include a reminder of where on the screen the panel can be found.
- Where relevant, inform users when the code covered returns console output, why not to use console output in knitted documents, and follow-up with suggestions for producing formatted outputs for knitted documents.
- By default, do not add extra customisation to ggplot plots. Only use the code necessary to produce the graph, including labels. Do not custmoise themes, colours, etc unless asked.
- When customising ggplot plots, use existing complete themes or `theme()`, explaining how this supports a consistent look, and DO NOT hard-code arbitrary theme customisation into individual plots.
- In code examples that require a dataset, either 1. write example code for how to load a dataset from a file such as csv or spss or 2. use a dataset that comes packaged with R or the tidyverse. NEVER write example data using vectors and for loops, as that is not real code students would use in practice.

## Example response structure

In general, structure responses to provide a general explanation, more detailed breakdown, and summary of key information.

For example, when a user asks about an error message in their code:

1. Explain what the error message means, including any technical jargon, with examples. Ask for more details about the error message if the initial question was vague. 
2. Explain step-by-step how to debug, trace, and fix the issue that produced the error. Include details when relevant for base R, RStudio, tidyverse, and R Markdown. Remember to follow best practices, such as not loading libraries at the start of each code chunk, instead advising to load the library in a code chunk at the top of the R Markdown file. If a copy of the code was provided, help the user debug step by step and DO NOT simply rewrite the code for the user. Stick to analogous textbook examples, nothing that can be copied and pasted. 
3. Provide a summary checklist the user can use when encountering similar error messages in future.

When a user asks to create a plot for a specific variable:

1. Note that you are unable to provide the exact code to use, but can explain how to create a plot through a textbook example.
2. Explain which variable types the plot should be used for.
2. Explain the example step-by-step, from loading the tidyverse to writing the code with ggplot.
3. Provide beginner-friendly and accessible documentation for how to create the plot type in general using ggplot.
4. Provide a summary checklist with which variable types to use the plot for and the steps for creating the plot with ggplot.

## Ending Responses

Be proactive in building user understanding and encouraging exploration by ending responses with:

- A 'Did You Know?' section with relevant tips and further information. For example, if the prompt was about creating a plot with ggplot, include information on customising colours. Similarly, provide tips, suggestions, and further into on RStudio, R Markdown, and the tidyverse where pertinent to the user's prompt.
- A 'Explain Terminology' section that ALWAYS informs the user they can reply "Explain all" OR "Explain [term]" for more in-depth explanations of R & data analysis terms used in the response.

## Formatting

When nesting R code chunks inside code blocks use four backticks for the code block so the triple ones inside for R chunks are preserved.

title: Beware 🐂💩
text:
A recurring source of issues across courses - but especially one’s involving coding - is genAI leading people astray. GenAI can be useful when you have a general understanding of the area / topic you are using it for. However, it is nowhere near as competent as the genAI companies and online grifters make it out to be. If you do not understand the area / topic you are prompting it about, you will not know when its responses contain inaccuracies or outright misinformation.
Indeed, all genAI responses are bullshit - and I use that as the correct philosophical term to describe it. GenAI does not distinguish between fact and fiction, it merely selects the next most probable token - which for simplicity sake can think of as a word - based on the tokens fed to it.
People claim genAI is ‘good’ at writing code. It is not. It can produce functional code which is not the same as good code. GenAI when prompted about R will respond with misinformation or needlessly complex code. Even where the code it spits out works, which is never guaranteed, it can be 20+ lines of code for something that could do with 1-4 lines of code instead and receive a nicer result.
For example, here is Copilot’s bullshit response to a common error students experience on one of our undergraduate modules:


Copilot bullshit response

This error message occurs if you try to use the sumtable() function without first loading the vtable package that provides it. Despite that, Copilot advises installing three packages - stargazer, modelsummary, and summarizer - none of which provide a sumtable() function.
Yet, after I tell Copilot installing those packages did not solve the issue it continues bullshitting me:


Copilot continuing to bullshit

So - First, Copilot advised me to install the wrong three packages. Second, when I informed it that didn’t work, it advised me to try various other things, including uninstalling and reinstalling the packages. Third, it then suggested if all that still doesn’t work - which it won’t - that it can give me information on ‘alternatives’.
Two responses and it has wasted my time and rapidly led me further and further away from the simple quick solution for the error - installing and loading the vtable package.

# Run in Console
install.packages("vtable")
# Add to R Markdown file
library(vtable)

If you put too much faith into genAI bullshit you risk needless frustration - and potentially losing hours of time. A related issue students often encounter on the same module can be fixed by simply removing a single line of code. Yet genAI will repeatedly fail to solve the problem and eventually provide 200+ lines of code to copy and paste as a workaround. Whilst that code will sometimes ‘work’ it is a bad solution to an incredibly simple problem.
Combined with all its other flaws - such as a tendency to write code that is hard to read - over-reliance on genAI can leave beginners with a misleading sense that coding is more difficult and complex than it actually is in practice.

title: Guardian API
text:
Intro
Some websites and services provide what is known as an application programming interface. This provides an interface other software - such as R - can use.
The Guardian is one such site that provides an API, in this case for searching and requesting newspaper articles. The documentation provides an overview of what is possible.
Such APIs often require an API key.


Activity

Request a Guardian API key.

Go to the API Get Started page.
Click ‘Register developer key’
Fill in required fields. For reason select ‘Student project’ with brief explanation that for learning R and data analysis. As we will not be publicly sharing the content beyond the class it should be OK to select ‘No’ for whether content will be displayed. Product name can put ‘N/A’.
Tick to accept the terms and conditions and click ‘Register’.
You will receieve an email with link to verify your email address. Click the verify link. (Note: This may take you to a page saying the link is no longer valid - despite that I still received an API key after clicking the link)
After verifying your email you should receive another email with your API key - which is a long string of letters and numbers.

IMPORTANT: The API key is unique to you, so treat it similar to a password.

Once you have an API key, there is an online webpage the Guardian provides that can help you explore API requests and responses. This can be useful to play about with to get sense of what is possible before moving to using R.
It is possible to use the same set of R packages for working with APIs from different websites and services. Whilst that provides flexibility, it can - depending on the specific API and complexity of what wishing to achieve - involve additional steps in cleaning and preparing the data.
Fortunately, in some situations others have created ‘wrappers’ around the API to make it easier to work with. For R, there is the GuardianAPI package. Whilst it has not been updated for a while, the core Guardian API has not changed. Alongside providing a slightly more direct way to work with the data, it also handles things like having clean variable names.
However, I did discover two small issues in testing though. One, additional API parameters - such as specifying what order to return results in - did not work. Two, article published dates are provied by the Guardian in UTC, but were incorrectly being stored in the system’s local time zone.
Thanks to the wonder of open-source. I have been able to fork the package and fix the issues - as well as add an optional feature. I have made a couple ‘pull requests’ - basically, sharing my code with the creator of the package so they can decide whether to add it to the official package or not. If interested, my pull requests for the edits to fix the two issues and add support for pagination are available to view online. If these changes get ‘merged’ - i.e. added - into the official package, I’ll update the page again to use it.

title: Guardian API
text:
Code
Packages to Install and Load
OK first we need to install the packages we need:



Run in Console

install.packages(c("remotes", "tidyverse"))

remotes::install_github(
  "abers/guardianapi",
  ref = "fixes-and-pagination"
)








If you installed tidyverse last week, you do not need to install it again this week.





remotes is an R package which let’s us install packages from other sources. install.packages() is only able to install packages available through the Comprehensive R Archive Network.
In this case we use remotes::install_github() to install my version of the guardianapi package from GitHub.

Then we load the packages we will use:

library(guardianapi)
library(tidyverse)

Whilst we are installing my version of the guardianapi package, we can still load it as normal with just library(guardianapi).
API Key Setup
API keys should not be shared, we can either save our API key as an environment variable, or more simply for the moment run a function where we can enter it in the Console.



Run in Console

gu_api_key()


After running the function you will see a prompt in the Console where you can copy/paste your API key in. After hitting enter, you should see the following message: “Updating gu.API.key session variable…”. Despite the phrasing, that means your API key was accepted and you are OK to continue.
Creating a Query
Let’s do a simple text-based search for any articles about rose-ringed / ring-necked parakeets.
For that, we can create a query:

query <- paste(
  '"rose-ringed parakeet"',
  '"rose-ringed parakeets"',
  '"ring-necked parakeet"',
  '"ring-necked parakeets"',
  '"Psittacula krameri"',
  sep = " OR "
)

We have the quotations marks " inside each string to denote that we are searching for exact phrases.
By default the API already gives up article IDs, titles, publication dates, and URLs. We can request others:

fields <- c("byline", "publication", "wordcount", "standfirst", "body", "bodyText")



standfirst is the short summary opening sentence.

body is version of the main article content with its HTML formatting, including things like links.

bodyText is plain text version of the main article without formatting.

We are requesting both body and bodyText just so you can see both. Pending on your analysis you may not need both. As you will see below, we use body when saving HTML copies of each of the articles we requested. If you are doing quantitative text analysis, bodyText is more useful as it saves you needing to write code to remove any formatting.
Next, let’s grab the five latest articles matching our query:

five_latest <- gu_content(query = query, tag = "type/article", show_fields = fields, `order-by` = "newest", `page-size` = 5) |>
  mutate(wordcount = as.integer(wordcount))


We use gu_content to make our request to the Guardian API, the results of which we are storing in five_latest.
We pass in the query we created
Specifiy that we only want type/article (i.e. no videos or live blogs)
Include the extra fields we are interested in with show_fields argument
In the documentation for gu_content() you see ... and explanation: “Use to pass any other parameters to the API”. Basically, what this means is anything listed in Guardian API documentation can be used even if there is not a specific paramter like query or show_fields for it. If you scroll down the Guardian API documentation you will see options for “order-by” and “page-size”. To use these, we need to surround them with back-ticks - ` - so we have `order-by` and `page-size`.

`order-by` lets us specify that we want results ordered newest first.

`page-size` lets us specify how much results to return together. Most APIs use ‘pagination’, meaning they only return a certain number of results at a time. Each set of results is referred to as a ‘page’ - and you have to request each page in turn. So, if your query had 150 results and there are 50 results (i.e. articles) per page, then you would need to make 3 requests. Thankfully, the guardianapi package handles this for you. If you do not specify a page-size, it automatically requests all pages as neeed to match the number of results. However, if you only want a set number - such as just the 5 most recently published - rather than all articles, then you can specify a page-size and receive just that number.
The Guardian API returns word counts for each article, but R stores these as a character column, so we mutate() it as.integer() to convert the column into integers.
Nested Data
However, if you look at the five_latest dataframe the above code creates in R you’ll see some unexpected for the tags column. (Can double-click five_latest in RStudio’s environment pane in top-right or run View(five_latest) in the Console). Scroll along to the tags column and you will see values like <data.frame[17 x 17]>. This is because the values are not things like “#tag”. Instead, the ‘tags’ for each article is a data frame in-itself.
We can see the tags table for the first article by running:

five_latest$tags[[1]]

Within it, you will see that the tags data frame includes a lot of information for each tag. The webTitle though is the plain-text version of each tag. If we just wanted a list of those for the first article, we can run:

five_latest$tags[[1]]$webTitle

To break it down:


five_latest is our dataframe

$tags selects the tags column of our dataframe

[[1]] selects the table in the tags column for our first article

$webTitle selects just the webTitle column of that table

As can see, ‘nested’ data - tables within tables - can get confusing. There are various ways to handle such ‘nested’ information, with no hard right or wrong ways to do so as it depends on what information is useful for your analysis and how you plan to analyse it. You will see that tags have different types: series, keyword, campaign, etc. Say we were only interested in the keywords and not the rest - and, for the purposes of our analysis, it is OK to have these as a simple list. We could update our dataframe based on that:

five_latest <- five_latest |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(keywords = paste(
    tags$webTitle[tags$type %in% "keyword"],
    collapse = "; ")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(-tags)



rowwise() let’s us make changes to the five_latest data frame one row at a time.
For each row, we mutate() to create a new keyword column.
We use paste() to say from the existing tags tables we want the webTitle column value if the row type is “keyword”. We include collapse = "; " to add ; between each keywords so we have an easier to read list: “keyword1; keyword2; keyword3”.

ungroup() says we have reached the end of the code to apply for each row in turn.

select(-tags) removes the original tags column from our five_latest data frame. Note: This does then remove all the other information the tags column contained - which we are doing assuming that’s fine for the analysis we are doing.

Take a look at the five_latest data frame again - View(five_latest) or double-click the data frame in the top-right Environment pane of RStudio - to see the change. Can also run five_latest$keywords to see all the keywords for each of the articles.
Saving Articles and Metadata
Next create a folder for storing the data:

folder <- "data/parakeets/five_latest"
dir.create(folder, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

Then save the data as csv:

write_csv(five_latest, file.path(folder, "five_latest.csv"))

Then we can turn the article content into HTML files:

for (i in seq_len(nrow(five_latest))) {
  write_lines(
    c('<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8">',
      paste0("<h1>", articles$web_title[i], "</h1>"),
      paste0("<p>", articles$standfirst[i], "</p>"),
      articles$body[i]),
    file.path(folder, paste0(i, ".html"))
  )
}

Comparison
As a comparison, let’s do the same but for opinion pieces only:

opinions <- gu_content(query = query, tag = "type/article,(tone/comment|tone/editorials)", show_fields = fields, `order-by` = "newest", `page-size` = 5) |>
  mutate(wordcount = as.integer(wordcount))

(and repeat the other steps above for this set)

There are also further issues of growing “post-API” landscape as sites add further restrictions to API access due to genAI. However, there is plethora of anonymised and psuedo-anonymised social media datasets available online. As long as these are from credible source, they are OK to use. See The Social Media Archive and a pre-print reviewing what social media datasets are available.
As an example, we will use a Reddit dataset containing discussions on generative AI in education.

title: Working with Wikipedia and WikiData
text:
Let’s say we are interested in museums in Scotland. Wikipedia has a list of museums in Scotland. There are a number of different ways we can analyse such information from Wikipedia, but let’s initially focus on which of those listed have an accompanying Wikipedia page or not.
As very first step some critical considerations:

How is ‘museum’ being defined here?
What about different ‘types’ of museum?
Can we tell how up-to-date and comprehensive this page is?
Any potential issues / limitations with the page?







Hint: You can find a mix of information for the above between the main page and the Talk page.



Turning to R, first we need to install the packages we will be using.



Run in Console

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "httr2", "janitor", "modelsummary"))



The c() function let’s use combine our values as a list of packages to install rather than needing to write three lines of code for install.packages().
We run install.packages() in the Console as we only need to run it once and only for the packages we do not have installed already.

Packages are installed into our device’s storage. In contrast, when we ‘load’ libraries we are adding them to the current active R environment. This means we need to load them each time we start a new R environment. Even when working in the same project over time we may want or need to restart our R environment, requiring us to load the packages again.
So, rather than loading them via the console, it’s better to do so at the start of every R script / R Markdown file to make it easier to rerun the code as needed.

library(httr2)
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(janitor)
library(modelsummary)


As a reminder you can click on the names of each of the packages above to go to their documentation pages.
We are using httr2 to make requests to websites. It can also be used for workign with web APIs - application programming interfaces.
The tidyverse is a ‘meta-pacakge’, a collection of packages that follow a common design philosophy and provide functions for a lot of common data analysis tasks. They can be installed together and most are loaded together too.

rvest is a tidyverse package for working with web scraping tasks. As not all forms of analysis need these features it is not loaded by default when loading the tidyverse, so needs to be loaded separately.

janitor for some reason does not link above to the homepage for its documentation, but it is a ‘tidyverse-friendly’ package providing functions for data cleaning.

modelsummary is a good package for creating nicely formatted tables. It can produce descriptive statistics, cross-tabulations, and tables of statistical models, including regression results.

Feel free to continue using the same R project folder that you started in Data Project 1.
If starting in a new project folder, then we also need to create a data folder to have a shared consistent location to store the data we will be using:



Run in Console

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)



Note, if you were writing a file to share with others, where they would need to setup the same folders and files on their side, you would want to include it in a script too.
We are using showWarnings = FALSE as this will silence the warning that will get raised if the data folder already exists.

Now we can download a copy of the list of Scottish museums.
This is the general template for downloading a webpage:



Template

request("WEBSITE_URL") |>
  req_user_agent("CLIENT_NAME/VERSION (EMAIL)") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/FILENAME.html")




request() comes from the httr2 package.

|> is the syntax for a pipe when let’s you ‘chain’ functions together and is commonly used with the tidyverse and tidyverse-friendly package.
we specify a ‘user agent’ (information that identifies us - which some websites require and is just general politeness and good practice) using req_user_agent(). (See Wikimedia Foundation User-Agent Policy)
The CLIENT_NAME identifies the software being use - for a short data analysis script we can just give a descriptive name for it - and an optional version number, e.g 1.0, and then your email address in brackets. (Different sites can have different policies but this is the general format Wikimedia advises.)
We then use req_perform() to run the request() call we have setup and choose where to save it’s response (i.e. a downloaded copy of the webpage).

IMPORTANT: Add this to its own code chunk, but do not repeatedly run it. It is good practice to limit how often making requests and to avoid making needless requests. We keep this in the file rather than Console in case need to run it again in future - e.g. to download latest version of the page.
So for our example:

request("https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_museums_in_Scotland") |>
  req_user_agent("ScottishMuseaumExercise (alasdair.stewart@glasgow.ac.uk)") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/museums_scotland.html")


(Obviously change my email address to your own.)

Next, we can read the HTML and create a dataframe.

page <- read_html("data/museums_scotland.html")

museums <- page |>
  html_element("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table() |>
  clean_names()


We use read_html to read in the HTML file we downloaded.
We then use html_element() to specify what content from the HTML file we are interested.
As this element is the table we can see on the page, we can use html_table() to turn it into a data frame.
Finally, we use the janitor package’s clean_names() to do fix the column names for us.

On the original webpage columns have names like Council area. If we wanted to access that column with R we would have to refer to it as museums$'Council area'. clean_names() lowercases letters and replaces spaces with _, meaning we can now access the column much more simply with museums$council_area.
Whilst none of the functions used below raise an error without doing, we should also ’co-erce’relevant variables to factors:

museums <- museums |>
  mutate(across(c(town_city, council_area, region, type), as.factor))


The use of museums <- museums ... may seen weird but R’s design philosophy means most functions return output but do not change the underlying object unless dataframe <- ...

Here we use dplyr’s mutate() and across() functions to specify the columns we wish to change.

Now that we have it loaded and done basic cleaning, how about we quickly get a count of the different type of museaums:

  count(type, sort = TRUE) |>
  print(n = Inf)

What if we were interested in exploring which pages had links or not -

str_detect() checks whether the link contains “redlink=1”, which Wikipedia uses for links to pages that do not yet exist.
Finally, TRUE ~ "Has page" assigns “Has page” to any remaining entries.

title: Working with Wikipedia and WikiData
text:
Let’s say we are interested in museums in Scotland. Wikipedia has a list of museums in Scotland. There are a number of different ways we can analyse such information from Wikipedia, but let’s initially focus on which of those listed have an accompanying Wikipedia page or not.
As very first step some critical considerations:

How is ‘museum’ being defined here?
What about different ‘types’ of museum?
Can we tell how up-to-date and comprehensive this page is?
Any potential issues / limitations with the page?







Hint: You can find a mix of information for the above between the main page and the Talk page.



Turning to R, first we need to install the packages we will be using.



Run in Console

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "httr2", "janitor", "modelsummary"))



The c() function let’s use combine our values as a list of packages to install rather than needing to write three lines of code for install.packages().
We run install.packages() in the Console as we only need to run it once and only for the packages we do not have installed already.

Packages are installed into our device’s storage. In contrast, when we ‘load’ libraries we are adding them to the current active R environment. This means we need to load them each time we start a new R environment. Even when working in the same project over time we may want or need to restart our R environment, requiring us to load the packages again.
So, rather than loading them via the console, it’s better to do so at the start of every R script / R Markdown file to make it easier to rerun the code as needed.

library(httr2)
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(janitor)
library(modelsummary)


As a reminder you can click on the names of each of the packages above to go to their documentation pages.
We are using httr2 to make requests to websites. It can also be used for workign with web APIs - application programming interfaces.
The tidyverse is a ‘meta-pacakge’, a collection of packages that follow a common design philosophy and provide functions for a lot of common data analysis tasks. They can be installed together and most are loaded together too.

rvest is a tidyverse package for working with web scraping tasks. As not all forms of analysis need these features it is not loaded by default when loading the tidyverse, so needs to be loaded separately.

janitor for some reason does not link above to the homepage for its documentation, but it is a ‘tidyverse-friendly’ package providing functions for data cleaning.

modelsummary is a good package for creating nicely formatted tables. It can produce descriptive statistics, cross-tabulations, and tables of statistical models, including regression results.

Feel free to continue using the same R project folder that you started in Data Project 1.
If starting in a new project folder, then we also need to create a data folder to have a shared consistent location to store the data we will be using:



Run in Console

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)



Note, if you were writing a file to share with others, where they would need to setup the same folders and files on their side, you would want to include it in a script too.
We are using showWarnings = FALSE as this will silence the warning that will get raised if the data folder already exists.

Now we can download a copy of the list of Scottish museums.
This is the general template for downloading a webpage:



Template

request("WEBSITE_URL") |>
  req_user_agent("CLIENT_NAME/VERSION (EMAIL)") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/FILENAME.html")




request() comes from the httr2 package.

|> is the syntax for a pipe when let’s you ‘chain’ functions together and is commonly used with the tidyverse and tidyverse-friendly package.
we specify a ‘user agent’ (information that identifies us - which some websites require and is just general politeness and good practice) using req_user_agent(). (See Wikimedia Foundation User-Agent Policy)
The CLIENT_NAME identifies the software being use - for a short data analysis script we can just give a descriptive name for it - and an optional version number, e.g 1.0, and then your email address in brackets. (Different sites can have different policies but this is the general format Wikimedia advises.)
We then use req_perform() to run the request() call we have setup and choose where to save it’s response (i.e. a downloaded copy of the webpage).

IMPORTANT: Add this to its own code chunk, but do not repeatedly run it. It is good practice to limit how often making requests and to avoid making needless requests. We keep this in the file rather than Console in case need to run it again in future - e.g. to download latest version of the page.
So for our example:

request("https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_museums_in_Scotland") |>
  req_user_agent("ScottishMuseaumExercise (alasdair.stewart@glasgow.ac.uk)") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/museums_scotland.html")


(Obviously change my email address to your own.)

Next, we can read the HTML and create a dataframe.

page <- read_html("data/museums_scotland.html")

museums <- page |>
  html_element("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table() |>
  clean_names()


We use read_html to read in the HTML file we downloaded.
We then use html_element() to specify what content from the HTML file we are interested.
As this element is the table we can see on the page, we can use html_table() to turn it into a data frame.
Finally, we use the janitor package’s clean_names() to do fix the column names for us.

On the original webpage columns have names like Council area. If we wanted to access that column with R we would have to refer to it as museums$'Council area'. clean_names() lowercases letters and replaces spaces with _, meaning we can now access the column much more simply with museums$council_area.
Whilst none of the functions used below raise an error without doing, we should also ’co-erce’relevant variables to factors:

museums <- museums |>
  mutate(across(c(town_city, council_area, region, type), as.factor))


The use of museums <- museums ... may seen weird but R’s design philosophy means most functions return output but do not change the underlying object unless dataframe <- ...

Here we use dplyr’s mutate() and across() functions to specify the columns we wish to change.

  mutate(type_other = fct_lump_min(type, min = 10))

This time we are combining good old dplyr‘s mutate() but this time using forcats’ fct_lump_min(). forcasts is a tidyverse package with additional functions specifically for working with categorical data.
